# Chapter Seventeen: Day Ninety-One

The email sat in Mara Voss's outbox like a loaded weapon.

*To: security@helixdynamics.com*
*Subject: Coordinated Disclosure — CVE Reservation Pending — Final Notice*

She'd drafted it eleven times over ninety days. Each version had gotten shorter, colder, more precise. This one was four sentences. It said everything that needed saying.

She hadn't sent it yet.

Outside her apartment window, Portland rained itself gray and indifferent. Three monitors glowed on her desk, casting blue light across a whiteboard crowded with diagrams — arrows, hash chains, a stick figure labeled *VICTIM* with a knife drawn toward it in red marker. The knife pointed at a box marked **HELIX-AUTH v4.2: SESSION REUSE FLAW**.

Ninety days. That was the industry standard, the courtesy window, the social contract between researchers and the companies whose software they broke. You find a hole in the world, you tell the people who own it, and you give them time to patch before the rest of the world learns it exists.

She'd found the hole on day zero. Reported it on day one. And then she'd watched Helix Dynamics do nothing.

Not exactly nothing. That was the part that kept her up at night.

---

Day nine: automated acknowledgment. *Thank you for your submission. Ticket #HD-4471 has been created.*

Day twenty-two: a human reply, finally. *We are evaluating the severity of this report and will follow up shortly.*

Day thirty-one: Mara's follow-up. No response.

Day forty: another follow-up. No response.

Day forty-four: she'd done the thing she hated doing — she'd gone public-adjacent, quietly, posting a sanitized teaser to a private mailing list of a dozen trusted researchers. *Anyone else looked at Helix's session token rotation? DM me.* Two replies. Both said the same thing: *Helix? Good luck. They ghost everyone.*

Day fifty-three: a voicemail from a number with a Redmond area code. A man named Colter, "Director of Product Security Assurance," a title she'd never heard before and couldn't find on LinkedIn. His voice was warm the way a handshake is warm — brief, performative, gone.

*"Dr. Voss. We're taking your report very seriously. There are complexities here you may not appreciate. I'd ask you to hold off on any disclosure timeline while we work through some... dependencies. Can you do that for me? As a professional courtesy."*

She had not agreed. She'd said, carefully, that ninety days was ninety days. He'd said, carefully, that he *heard* her. Neither of them had believed the other.

Day sixty-one: her threat-intelligence feeds lit up with something that made her stomach drop. A ransomware crew she'd been tracking — VANTABLACK, the ones who'd hit the hospital network in Rotterdam — had started scanning for Helix authentication endpoints. Not exploiting yet. *Mapping.*

The flaw she'd found wasn't theoretical. It let an attacker replay a captured session token across Helix's single-sign-on fabric — the glue that held together hospital records systems, payroll platforms, two regional utilities. One stolen token, reused silently, indefinitely, because Helix's rotation scheme had a race condition that invalidated nothing. It was a master key that never wore out.

She'd told them that in her first report. She'd included a proof of concept that required physical access, deliberately hobbled. She'd offered to help write the patch.

Day sixty-eight: Colter called again. This time he didn't sound warm.

*"Dr. Voss, I need you to understand the legal posture here. If this disclosure causes harm to our customers, our counsel will view that as a knowing and voluntary act. I'd hate for this to become a matter for attorneys."*

*"Are you threatening me?"*

*"I'm educating you."* A pause. *"There are dependencies you don't understand. Embedded deployments. Legacy contracts. Patching this is not a switch we can flip."*

*"It's been sixty-eight days."*

*"And we appreciate your patience."*

The call ended, and Mara sat in the dark of her apartment and did the math that researchers always end up doing: the math of what happens if she's wrong. If she discloses and VANTABLACK weaponizes it before the patch lands, someone in a hospital in Rotterdam or Reno or wherever dies because of her advisory. Her name on the CVE. Her decision.

And the other math: what happens if she stays silent. Because the scanners were still running. Because silence wasn't neutral — silence was just a head start you gave to whoever found it next, and next time it wouldn't be someone who wrote a hobbled proof of concept and offered to help.

---

Now it was day ninety-one
